title: La estantería de los videobooks  (The Showreel Shelf)

segments.t: Back in the PS Management office, Paquita shows off the shelf where hopeful actors send their showreels by courier. As she and Magüi browse through old reels, Paquita passionately defends the wealth of acting talent in Spain and praises stars known by a single first name like Carmen. Listen to the Spanish first.
Esta es la estantería de los videobooks.
Vienen a veces a dejarlos por mensajería.
Ha llegado el momento de verlos.
Mira el de Miguel Ángel Muñoz.
Empezó con nosotros.
Hay muchísimo talento en España.
Que no os engañen.
Está bien elegida la foto.
Es importante la gente que solo se pone un nombre.
¿Qué Carmen es?
Carmen Sevilla.
Solo dices Carmen y ya sabes de quién se habla.
Let's walk through what Paquita and Magüi say at the showreel shelf.
Esta es la estantería de los videobooks.

'This is the shelf of showreels.' Built from the word for "shelf", the longer feminine word here means a whole bookcase or shelving unit. Spanish casting agencies borrow the English compound "videobook" for an actor's video showreel.
Vienen a veces a dejarlos por mensajería.

'Sometimes people come to drop them off by courier.' Literally "they come at times to leave them by courier", using plural "they come" without naming who, where English says "people come". Notice how "them" tacks right onto the end of "to leave".
Ha llegado el momento de verlos.

'The time has come to watch them.' Literally "has arrived the moment of to see them", putting "has arrived" ahead of "the moment". At the end, the little word for "them" attaches directly onto "to see" as one smooth word.
Mira el de Miguel Ángel Muñoz.

'Look at Miguel Ángel Muñoz's one.' Instead of adding an apostrophe-s to the actor's name, Spanish says "the of Miguel Ángel Muñoz", letting masculine "the" stand in for "the showreel" without repeating the word.
Empezó con nosotros.
'He started out with us.' The stressed -ó ending marks a completed past event for "he" or "she", so no separate word for "he" is needed. After "with", Spanish uses the full plural word for "us".
Hay muchísimo talento en España.
'There is tons of talent in Spain.' Adding the intensifying ending -ísimo onto "much" boosts it from "a lot of" to "tons of" or "so much", matching the masculine singular ending of "talent".
Que no os engañen.

'Don't let them fool you.' Starting with "that" plus "not" creates an emphatic warning, literally "that they not deceive you all". In Spain, the little two-letter word before "fool" is the casual plural "you" addressed to everyone watching.
Está bien elegida la foto.

'The photo is well chosen.' Even though the clipped everyday word for "photo" ends in -o, it stays feminine because it is short for "photograph", so "chosen" takes the feminine -an ending. Putting "the photo" at the end highlights the praise "is well chosen" first.
Es importante la gente que solo se pone un nombre.

'People who only use one name are important.' Because the collective word for "people" is grammatically singular, "is important" stays singular too. Towards the end, "puts on oneself a name" is the natural Spanish idiom for adopting a stage name.
¿Qué Carmen es?
'Which Carmen is it?' Right before a name or thing, the simple word for "what" does the job of English "which", asking Paquita to narrow down which famous Carmen she means.
Carmen Sevilla.
'Carmen Sevilla.' Paquita names legendary Spanish actress, singer, and television presenter Carmen Sevilla, whose stage surname comes from her home city of Sevilla rather than her family name.
Solo dices Carmen y ya sabes de quién se habla.

'You just say Carmen and you already know who people mean.' Spanish never strands "of" or "about" at the end of a question clause, saying "of whom" together rather than "who ... about". Then "itself speaks" works as an impersonal way to say "people are talking". Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Esta es la estantería de los videobooks.
Vienen a veces a dejarlos por mensajería.
Ha llegado el momento de verlos.
Mira el de Miguel Ángel Muñoz.
Empezó con nosotros.
Hay muchísimo talento en España.
Que no os engañen.
Está bien elegida la foto.
Es importante la gente que solo se pone un nombre.
¿Qué Carmen es?
Carmen Sevilla.
Solo dices Carmen y ya sabes de quién se habla.
You heard how Spanish borrows 'videobook' for an actor's showreel, how 'the one of' stands in for apostrophe-s, and how 'itself speaks' expresses 'people mean'. See you next time.
¡Nos vemos!
